title: Salzburg & Vienna Trivia
subtitle: How much do you know about your trip? 5–12 December 2026
coverAlt: Salzburg's old town by the river, with snowy mountains behind

photos.label: The car at the Military History Museum

questions.q: Your plane lands in Munich. Which country is Munich in?
questions.h: It's next door to Austria, and you take a train across the border.
questions.f: You start your trip in Germany and cross into Austria by train. Two countries before lunch!

questions.q: What money will you spend in Austria?
questions.h: It's the same money used in Germany, France and Spain.
questions.f: Austria uses the euro. Coins have a different picture on the back in each country, but they all work everywhere.

questions.q: Which language do most people speak in Austria?
questions.h: It's the same language they speak in Munich.
questions.f: There's no language called Austrian! People speak German, with some words of their own.

questions.q: In Austria, “Servus” can mean both hello AND goodbye.
questions.h: Austrians like a word that does two jobs.
questions.f: Servus is a friendly hi and bye in Austria and southern Germany. Try it on a shopkeeper!

questions.q: What number do you call for help anywhere in Europe?
questions.h: It's not the number you'd call at home in the US.
questions.f: 112 works in every European Union country, even from a phone with no SIM card.

questions.q: About how long is the nonstop flight from San Francisco to Munich?
questions.h: Long enough to sleep through the night on the plane.
questions.f: The flight leaves in the afternoon and lands the next morning, so you skip a night. That's jet lag.
questions.note: UA194 timing from the trip page, checked 30 Sep

questions.q: Kids under 15 ride the Westbahn train from Salzburg to Vienna for free.
questions.h: Think about who pays on this train when you travel with your parents.
questions.f: On Westbahn, children under 15 travel free with an adult, so your ticket costs nothing.
questions.note: Westbahn child fare, from the trip page

questions.q: Which famous composer was born in Salzburg?
questions.h: His first name is Wolfgang.
questions.f: Mozart was born in 1756 at Getreidegasse 9, just around the corner from your hotel.

questions.q: How old was Mozart when he started making up his own music?
questions.h: Younger than you are now. Much younger!
questions.f: At five he was composing little pieces and playing them to his dad, who wrote them down.

questions.q: “Salz” is the German word for something that made Salzburg rich. What is it?
questions.h: You put it on your fries.
questions.f: Boats carrying salt down the river paid a toll here 1,300 years ago. You'll see where it came from on Tuesday.

questions.q: This castle sits on a hill high above Salzburg. What is it called?
questions.h: Its name has the city's name hiding inside it.
questions.f: People started building it in 1077. It's one of the biggest castles from the Middle Ages in all of Europe.

questions.q: When the little railway up to the fortress opened in 1892, what made it move?
questions.h: The car going down was made heavier so it could pull the other one up.
questions.f: The car at the top filled a tank with water. The extra weight sent it down and pulled the other car up.

questions.q: The Christmas market is on Domplatz. What does “Dom” mean in German?
questions.h: Look for the giant church with the green domes next to the stalls.
questions.f: The market sits right in front of Salzburg Cathedral, and it's lit up best after dark.

questions.q: At the Christmas markets, kids can drink “Kinderpunsch”. What is it?
questions.h: It's warm, and it smells like oranges and cinnamon.
questions.f: Kinder means children, and Kinderpunsch has no alcohol in it. Grown-ups drink a version that does.
questions.note: from the trip page's market notes

questions.q: Your market drink comes in a real mug. What happens when you give the mug back?
questions.h: You paid a little extra for the mug when you bought the drink.
questions.f: That extra is a deposit, about 4 or 5 euros. Or keep the mug as a souvenir!
questions.note: mug deposit, from the trip page

questions.q: Which famous singing movie was filmed in Salzburg?
questions.h: Seven children, a nanny called Maria, and a song about a few of her favorite things.
questions.f: It came out in 1965 and was the biggest movie of that year. Tours still visit the places it was filmed.

questions.q: Café Tomaselli, where you might have hot chocolate if it snows, is more than 300 years old.
questions.h: It's known as the oldest café in Salzburg.
questions.f: It was serving coffee in the early 1700s, before Mozart was even born.
questions.note: founding date not on English Wikipedia; trip page calls it the city's oldest café

questions.q: In Salzburg in December, about what time does the sun go down?
questions.h: Earlier than you'd finish school.
questions.f: December days are short in Austria. That's why the trip has you at the Christmas markets in the dark.
questions.note: 16:16 sunset from the trip page's daylight table

questions.q: On Monday you go up this snowy mountain to play on a glacier. What is a glacier?
questions.h: It's so big and heavy that it slowly slides downhill.
questions.f: Glacier ice is very slowly flowing downhill all the time, even while you're standing on it.

questions.q: The top station on the Kitzsteinhorn is about how high?
questions.h: Higher than the tallest building in the world, but not as high as a plane flies.
questions.f: That's almost 10,000 feet. Stack about nine Eiffel Towers on top of each other and you're there.

questions.q: At the top of the glacier, it's warmer than in Salzburg because you're closer to the sun.
questions.h: Think about why mountaintops have snow on them.
questions.f: The higher you go, the colder it gets. Up top it can be around 25 °F colder than in town.
questions.note: the ~14 °C difference is derived from altitude on the trip page, not a published figure

questions.q: The Kitzsteinhorn was the first place in Austria where people could ski on what?
questions.h: It's the thing you're going up there to see.
questions.f: The first cable car opened in 1965 and made it Austria's first glacier ski area.

questions.q: In the salt mine, how do you get down to the lower tunnels?
questions.h: It's the fastest, most fun way down. Whee!
questions.f: The miners' slides are long and smooth. You sit on two wooden rails and zoom down.

questions.q: Deep inside the mine there's an underground lake. How do you cross it?
questions.h: You'll stay dry, but you'll be floating.
questions.f: The boat trip across the lake in the dark is one of the last things you do before leaving the mine.

questions.q: Inside the salt mine you can walk underground from Austria into Germany.
questions.h: The mountain doesn't know where the border is.
questions.f: The mine runs right under the border. In 1829 the two countries signed a treaty about it.

questions.q: How do you ride into the salt mine at the start?
questions.h: It runs on tracks, like the miners used.
questions.f: An electric miners' train takes you about 400 meters into the mountain.

questions.q: Vienna is the capital city of which country?
questions.h: It's the country you're already in when you get on the train.
questions.f: Vienna is Austria's biggest city. In German it's called Wien.

questions.q: On Wednesday night you can go ice skating in front of the Rathaus. What is a Rathaus?
questions.h: It's where the mayor works.
questions.f: Vienna's city hall has a tower almost 100 meters tall, and a giant Christmas market in front.

questions.q: The zoo you visit on Thursday holds a world record. What is it?
questions.h: Think about how long ago emperors lived in the palace next door.
questions.f: Schönbrunn Zoo opened in 1752, more than 270 years ago, and it's still open today.

questions.q: Schönbrunn is one of only a few zoos in the world with these animals. What are they?
questions.h: They're black and white and they love bamboo.
questions.f: Only about 27 zoos in the whole world have giant pandas.
questions.note: pandas move between zoos; confirm they're at Schönbrunn in December 2026

questions.q: Emperors and empresses spent their summers in this huge yellow palace. What is it?
questions.h: You visit its zoo on the same day.
questions.f: It was the summer home of Austria's royal family, the Habsburgs.

questions.q: About how many rooms does Schönbrunn Palace have?
questions.h: More rooms than a hotel. Lots more.
questions.f: It has 1,441 rooms. Your tour only shows a few of them, which is plenty!

questions.q: On Friday evening you can ride this. What is it?
questions.h: It goes round and round, slowly, high in the sky.
questions.f: It's called the Riesenrad, which means giant wheel. It's about 65 meters tall.

questions.q: When was Vienna's giant wheel built?
questions.h: Your great-great-grandparents could have ridden it when it was new.
questions.f: From 1920 to 1985 it was the tallest Ferris wheel still standing anywhere in the world.

questions.q: The old car in Vienna's Military History Museum is famous because of what happened in it in 1914. What did that start?
questions.h: Something very big and very sad that lasted four years.
questions.f: An archduke was riding in this car when he was attacked. A few weeks later the First World War began.

questions.q: Vienna is famous for a chocolate cake. What is it called?
questions.h: Its name ends in “torte”, the German word for a fancy cake.
questions.f: It's chocolate cake with a thin layer of apricot jam inside and shiny chocolate on top.

questions.q: The story goes that Sachertorte was invented by a teenager.
questions.h: He was still learning to be a cook at the time.
questions.f: The story says Franz Sacher made it in 1832, when he was about 16 and still an apprentice.
questions.note: Wikipedia gives this as 'one story', not settled fact

questions.q: If it rains, you might visit the Natural History Museum. What can you see there?
questions.h: Things from a very, very long time ago, and some from space.
questions.f: The rainy-day plan says it's ten minutes away on the subway. It's closed on Tuesdays.
questions.note: from the trip page's bad-weather plan
